keyboard_models:
I added both keyboards to a copy of the package's MuJoCo model. The robot itself is unchanged: same GLB convex hulls, 368 g, MG90S servos limited to 0.20 N·m and 600°/s with back-EMF droop, the coupled hip limit, 0.5 ms timestep. Mesh-on-mesh contact uses multiccd, so a paw resting on a keycap gets several contact points. The package in yeni/paket/B was not modified. Scripts are in klavye/tarcin/kb/kbd.py and kbsim.py.

K1, laptop chiclet keyboard (a 15.6" laptop with a numpad):
- Deck (laptop base) 380 x 221 mm, 8-12 mm above the desk.
- 101 caps on a 19.05 mm pitch. Tops are 15-16 mm square, so the gaps are 3-4 mm. Caps stand 1.5-2.0 mm proud of the deck.
- Half-height F row. An open lid stands behind the keys, leaning 20° back.

K2, full-size ANSI 104-key mechanical keyboard:
- Key area 428.6 x 123.8 mm. The case is a wedge: plate 19-22 mm above the desk at the front, tilted 4-6° so the back is about 29-34 mm up.
- Caps are tapered (18 mm at the base, 13-14 mm tops, so 5-6 mm gaps at the top). Tops sit 7-10 mm above the plate, with OEM-style sculpt steps of 0-2 mm between rows. Together with the tilt, the visible step between rows is up to about 3.7 mm.
- 6.25u space bar, 2u tall + and Enter, 0.25u gaps between key blocks, Esc and F-row gaps.
- Real nav-cluster holes: a 3u x 1u hole at the home row and 1u holes beside the up arrow, 7-10 mm deep.

Each keyboard comes in two versions:
- 'Real' (actual size) is used for walking along the rows.
- A 'field' version repeats the rows three keyboards deep (on K2 the tilt continues). It is used for the diagonal runs (30/45/135/150/210/225/315/330° to the rows) so that a 25 cm path fits.

Test conditions:
- Keycap and deck friction 0.3, 0.4 and 0.6 (the paws touch keys at that value). The desk stays at the package's 0.6, with 0.9 for the TPU paws.
- 12 random starts per terrain x heading x friction = 36 runs per cell, 144 keyboard runs per gait, plus 20 flat-desk runs.
- The robot starts already standing on the keys, with at least 35 % of every paw sole on a key top. Start offset along the row, lateral position ±10-14 mm, and yaw ±3° are random. Heading is along +x or -x for the row runs.

Failure rules:
- Success means covering 25 cm.
- Fell: tilt over 45° or the body collapsing.
- Stuck: a paw moved less than 3 mm in 3 s, or the body made less than 10 mm progress in 3 s.
- Off: any paw down on the desk.
- Timeout: 30 s.

The training and sweep seeds (100+, 200+, 300+) are separate from the test seeds (0-11).
baseline_result:
The package trot exactly as built: 0.52 s period, 20 mm stride, 5.3 mm lift, IMU levelling, no heading hold.

- K1 laptop: 72/72. Along the rows 36/36 at 7.3-8.8 cm/s, diagonal 36/36 at 7.4-8.2 cm/s, sideways drift only about 3.5 mm per 100 mm.
- K2 mechanical, along the rows: 0/36. 31 runs fell after the robot drifted downhill off the front edge; the drift is about 100 mm sideways per 100 mm forward (median), usually within 3-7 cm of travel. 5 runs fell or stuck in the nav-cluster holes.
- K2 diagonal: 14/36 (3/12 at friction 0.3, 5/12 at 0.4, 6/12 at 0.6). 18 of the 22 failures happened going uphill, with the paw toe stubbing on rising row edges or the robot falling.
- Flat desk: 20/20 at 7.2-7.7 cm/s.
- Climbing onto K1 (8-10.5 mm deck step): 5/8. Climbing onto K2 (18-21 mm case edge): 0/8, and no paw ever got up.

Why the package trot hits a wall:
- The 5 mm lift is almost the mechanical maximum. With the stock stance, the front and hind leg pods on the same side touch at 8 mm lift and overlap 4 mm at 15 mm lift (they have 1.6 mm clearance at 5 mm).
- The paw is a flat 17 x 21 mm puck with a vertical toe face. It only has about 1 mm of edge rounding, so it catches on any edge higher than about 2 mm.
best_gait:
No gait on the unchanged hardware walks the tilted mechanical keyboard. The 'rough-terrain trot' below is the best I found, and it only matches the package trot. I did not find a high-lift gait that works.

Rough-terrain trot (RT), same hardware:
- Same 0.52 s period, 20 mm stride and 5.3 mm lift.
- Spread stance: front feet 16 mm forward, hind feet 16 mm back, body 4 mm lower. This removes the pod collisions (pod clearance becomes 6.7 mm even at 15 mm lift).
- Package IMU levelling, plus gyro heading hold (differential stride, gain 0.8, limit ±8 mm).
- Results: K1 72/72 at 5.0-7.3 cm/s, K2 rows 0/36, K2 diagonal 13/36. Flat desk 19/20 at 4.9-6.9 cm/s.

Higher foot lift (12-25 mm) does not work on this robot:
- Sweep of 45 combinations: lift 5.3/8/11/14/18 mm x stance spread 0/10/16 mm x period 0.42/0.52/0.65 s.
- At 14 mm lift the trot usually falls even on the flat desk. At 18 mm it fell in 3/3 flat runs for every period and spread.
- Knee saturation rises from 12 % at 5 mm to 36-44 % at 14-18 mm.
- RT8 (8 mm lift, 0.65 s period): K1 68/72, K2 rows 0/36, K2 diagonal 12/36, flat 19/20 at 3.5-5.5 cm/s.

Walk, one leg at a time (WALK):
- 1.0 s period, duty 0.8, 12 mm lift, 12 mm stance spread, 12 mm fore-aft body sway, gentler levelling.
- Results: K1 72/72 but only 1.9-2.3 cm/s, K2 rows 0/36, K2 diagonal 10/36, flat 20/20 at 2.5-2.7 cm/s.
- A slower walk (1.6 s period) did not move forward, even on the flat desk.
- Why: the centre of mass is 6.4 mm ahead of the body centre at hip height, and the legs only swing forward and back (no sideways joint). In a static test, lifting one front paw 10-15 mm tips the body 12-19°, even with the body shifted 10-15 mm back.

Search tools:
- An adapted search_kb.py (64 random candidates plus 4 ES iterations around the package trot, 14 training runs per candidate) found nothing more than 1/14 better than the package trot.
- Stopping the levelling, longer duty, and uphill crab control (kc or a fixed crab angle) did not fix the K2 drift. A fixed uphill crab made the paws step off the case edge in every run (36/36).

Best overall, with a mechanical change (MECH):
- Paws moved 25 mm further out (paw centres at ±48 mm instead of ±23 mm), plus rounded twin-capsule 'ski' soles, plus RT with 8 mm lift.
- Results: K1 72/72 at 6.7-8.7 cm/s. K2 diagonal 30/36 (9/9/12 at friction 0.3/0.4/0.6). K2 rows 2/36. Flat 20/20 at 5.5 cm/s.
- It holds up with a sagging battery: at 0.16 N·m it gets K2 diagonal 28/36, K1 72/72, flat 6/6.

The robot has only about 25-40 mm of sideways room on a 124 mm deep keyboard, so anything above about 10-15 mm per 100 mm walks off within 25 cm. Drift is also lower on a plain 5° slope with friction 1.0 (20-30 mm per 250 mm, against 107-171 at friction 0.4). Drift is not a contact-model artifact: it persisted with elliptic friction cones and noslip iterations.

servo_loads:
The simulated servo can never exceed its 0.20 N·m clamp, so peak torque is always 0.200 whenever a joint saturates. The useful numbers are the median, p95, and the share of time at the limit (above 0.195 N·m), split into stance (foot loaded) and swing (foot moving). They come from torques.py, and the batch tables give per-cell p95 and saturation.

Package trot (BASE):
- Flat desk: hip stance median 0.031, p95 0.115 N·m, 0 % at the limit (about 40 % margin at p95). Knee stance median 0.031, p95 0.136, 2 % at the limit. Knee swing p95 0.200, at the limit 10 % of swing time.
- K1: hip p95 0.11-0.12 with no time at the limit; knee p95 about 0.20 with 5-6 % at the limit.
- K2: everything is at the limit. Hip p95 0.20 (6-8 %), knee swing at the limit 25 % before it falls.

RT: flat hip p95 0.15 (2 %), knee 3-5 %. On keyboards, hip p95 0.13-0.19 and knee at the limit 3-8 %.

WALK: stance loads are low (knee median 0.026), but the fast 12 mm swing keeps the knee at the limit 42-48 % of swing time. The MG90S cannot follow that swing.

MECH: flat hip and knee p95 0.200, hip at the limit 5 %, knee 9 % (stance medians 0.05). On K1, hip at the limit 5-8 % and knee 11-12 %. On K2, knee swing at the limit up to 27 %. Even so, MECH still worked at 0.16 N·m (K2 diagonal 28/36).

Main point: the weight-bearing load is small (median 0.03-0.06 N·m, 15-30 % of the limit). The knees hit the limit while swinging the leg fast, and on K2 also on impacts and stumbles. Higher lifts mainly increase knee saturation: at 0.52 s period and no spread, 12 % at 5.3 mm, 21 % at 8, 28 % at 11, 36 % at 14 and 44 % at 18 mm. That, not the weight, is why higher steps destabilise the trot.
climb_onto_keyboard:
- Onto a laptop deck (8-12 mm): possible. The package trot climbed it 5/8, MECH 6/8, and MECH with 20 mm longer shins 8/8, in 2-5 s.
- Onto a full-size mechanical keyboard: not possible with this body, 0/8 for every gait, build and scripted move I tried. The front case edge is 18-21 mm high and the first cap row 7-10 mm above that.
  - The stock leg pods hang only 16 mm above the desk. When the hind paws reach the wall, the hind pods hit its top edge.
  - Even with 20 mm longer shins, a wide track and a 22 mm high-step trot, at best 3 of 4 paws got up; a hind paw never did.
  - A scripted 'rear up and put both front paws on the rim' sequence tipped the robot over in every attempt.
verdict:
Honest answer: Tarçın walks on a laptop (chiclet) keyboard, but not on a tilted full-size mechanical keyboard, and changing the gait does not fix that.

Laptop keyboard (K1): fine already. The existing 5 mm trot succeeds 72/72 at every friction (0.3-0.6) at 7-9 cm/s, and it climbs a 8-10.5 mm laptop deck 5/8. On this hardware the earlier claim that it "can't even walk on a keyboard" is true only for mechanical keyboards.

Mechanical keyboard (K2):
- Walking along the rows fails for every gait: 0/36.
  - The 4-6° tilt and the stepped, tapered caps make the light trotting robot slip downhill sideways about 100 mm per 100 mm forward.
  - It falls or steps off the front edge after 3-15 cm. A full-size keyboard also has 7-10 mm deep holes around the arrow and nav keys.
  - Diagonally on a large key field it manages 10-14/36.
- No rough-terrain gait fixes this on the unchanged robot.
  - Lifting the feet 12-25 mm makes the trot fall even on the flat desk.
  - Same-side leg pods collide at about 8 mm lift unless the stance is spread.
  - One-leg-at-a-time walking cannot balance, because the legs only swing forward and back and the centre of mass sits ahead of the body centre at hip height.
  - Heading hold, levelling changes and uphill 'crabbing' do not remove the sideways drift.

Mechanical changes, in order of effect (simulated):
1. Wider paw track: shins and paws 25 mm further out on each side (paw centres at ±48 mm instead of ±23 mm). This needs a pod/shin redesign, because the shin would come out under the pod centre. It is the change that matters most: K2 diagonal goes from 14 to 25/36, and to 30/36 with the next item.
2. Rounded 'ski' paw soles in place of the vertical-toed puck. Small effect alone (11/36); helpful together with the wide track.
3. Silicone pads (friction about 1.0). These halve the sideways drift: K2 along the rows goes from 2 to 9/36.
4. Longer shins (+20 mm). These do not help walking on K2 (23/36 diagonal). They make the laptop climb reliable (8/8) but still cannot climb onto K2.
5. 'Lower body' is not available: the pods already hang only 16 mm above the desk.

Even with items 1-3 together, walking along a real, tilted 124 mm deep mechanical keyboard stays unreliable (2-9/36): the robot still drifts 15-35 mm sideways per 10 cm and has no way to sense or correct its sideways position. A reliable K2 walker needs sideways foot placement (a hip roll servo per leg, i.e. 4 more servos) or a sensor that sees the keyboard edges. That would be a different robot.

Practical advice for the family: buy the robot as designed if 'on the laptop keyboard' is enough. Do not promise walking across a mechanical keyboard. Silicone pads plus the wider-track leg redesign get the diagonal case to about 80 % in simulation, but not along the rows.

Caveats: these are simulation results (convex hulls, simplified tapered keycaps, chaotic outcomes, ±2-3/36 noise between reruns), so expect ±30 % on hardware.
